# Optimized high-level model for Exo FDTD-2D

domain:
    # Time and space dimensions (values provided at runtime)
    t: dim in [0, tmax)        # time steps
    i: dim in [0, nx)          # x-direction (row index)
    j: dim in [0, ny)          # y-direction (column index)

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored in row-major order: element (i,j) at offset i*ny + j.
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * ny + j      # electric field component Ex
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * ny + j      # electric field component Ey
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * ny + j      # magnetic field component Hz

    # 1D fictitious source array, contiguous in memory
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t                    # only read, never modified

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (passed from driver; must match the domain bounds)
    tmax: size
    nx:   size
    ny:   size

    # Physical update coefficients; to exactly match the given code choose:
    #   c_ey = 0.5, c_ex = 0.5, c_hz = 0.7
    c_ey: DATA_TYPE
    c_ex: DATA_TYPE
    c_hz: DATA_TYPE

    # Tuning knobs for the optimized schedule (chosen empirically for the target machine).
    # Typical values on a modern x64 with large LLC:
    #   TI ≈ 32–128 (rows per tile), TJ ≈ 64–256 (columns per tile),
    #   V  = SIMD width in elements (e.g., 4 for AVX2 float, 8 for AVX2 double).
    TI: size    # tile size in i (x) dimension
    TJ: size    # tile size in j (y) dimension
    V:  size    # vector length along j (must divide TJ or be handled with scalar cleanup)

computation:
    # Explicit FDTD time-stepping loop. This must remain sequential in t because
    # each step depends on hz, ex, ey from the previous time step.
    for t in seq(0, tmax):

        # 1) Ey boundary condition along i = 0:
        #    ey(0, j) is overwritten from the fictitious source for time t.
        ey_bc:
            for j in [0, ny):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2) Interior Ey update for i >= 1:
        #    Uses the current Hz field; Hz is read-only in this phase.
        ey_update:
            for i in [1, nx):
                for j in [0, ny):
                    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_ey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3) Interior Ex update for j >= 1:
        #    Also uses the current Hz field and does not modify Hz.
        ex_update:
            for i in [0, nx):
                for j in [1, ny):
                    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - c_ex * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4) Hz update on interior cells (0 <= i < nx-1, 0 <= j < ny-1):
        #    Uses the updated Ex and Ey from this same time step.
        hz_update:
            for i in [0, nx - 1):
                for j in [0, ny - 1):
                    hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - c_hz * (
                        (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                        (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                    )

dependencies:
    # Time-stepping is a sequential recurrence:
    # all updates at time t+1 depend on the completed Hz update at time t.
    for t in [0, tmax - 1]:
        hz_update(t) -> ey_bc(t + 1)
        hz_update(t) -> ey_update(t + 1)
        hz_update(t) -> ex_update(t + 1)
        hz_update(t) -> hz_update(t + 1)

    # Within a single time step, the order of the four phases must be preserved:
    for t in [0, tmax):
        ey_bc(t)     -> ey_update(t)   # boundary ey[0,*] must be ready before interior Ey uses it (via Hz in later steps)
        ey_update(t) -> hz_update(t)   # Hz uses updated Ey
        ex_update(t) -> hz_update(t)   # Hz uses updated Ex

optimization:
    # The computation is memory-bandwidth bound and operates over large 2D grids.
    # We therefore optimize primarily for cache locality, SIMD utilization, and
    # multi-core parallelism, while keeping the time dimension strictly sequential.

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. 2D spatial blocking (tiling) of the i,j loops inside each time step
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Apply the same tiling to all spatial loops in ey_update, ex_update, and
    # hz_update. Conceptually, for each such loop nest:
    #
    #   for i in [lo_i, hi_i):
    #       for j in [lo_j, hi_j):
    #           body(i,j)
    #
    # becomes:
    #
    #   for I in [0, ceil((hi_i - lo_i) / TI)):
    #       for J in [0, ceil((hi_j - lo_j) / TJ)):
    #           for i in [lo_i + I*TI, min(hi_i, lo_i + (I+1)*TI)):
    #               for j in [lo_j + J*TJ, min(hi_j, lo_j + (J+1)*TJ)):
    #                   body(i,j)
    #
    # This keeps tiles of ex/ey/hz small enough to fit into cache and improves
    # spatial locality, especially when the full grid is larger than LLC.
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # Hoist the tile loops so they are the outermost spatial loops within each
    # time step:  for t, for I, for J, for i, for j, ...
    # This ensures that we iterate over tiles systematically and reuse each
    # tile across ey_update, ex_update, and hz_update within the same t
    # before moving on to the next region of the grid.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Thread-level parallelism over tiles
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within a single time step, all points in the spatial domain are
    # mutually independent inside each of the three update phases (ey_update,
    # ex_update, hz_update), because:
    #   - Hz is read-only in ey_update and ex_update,
    #   - Ex and Ey are read-only in hz_update,
    #   - there are no within-phase dependencies between different (i,j).
    #
    # Therefore, tiles indexed by I (and/or J) can be executed in parallel.
    # We choose to parallelize over I to obtain coarse-grain parallelism with
    # good cache locality along rows. This maps naturally to OpenMP-style
    # loop parallelization.
    parallelize(I)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. SIMD vectorization along the contiguous j dimension
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Memory layout is row-major, so elements differing in j are contiguous.
    # All inner loops over j access ex[i,*], ey[i,*], hz[i,*] with unit stride.
    #
    # In ey_update and ex_update, there are no data dependencies along j:
    #   - ey[i,j] depends only on hz[i,j] and hz[i-1,j],
    #   - ex[i,j] depends only on hz[i,j] and hz[i,j-1].
    #
    # In hz_update, we read ex[i,j] and ex[i,j+1], ey[i,j] and ey[i+1,j]; the
    # fields themselves are not modified within hz_update, so vector lanes
    # remain independent.
    #
    # Hence vectorization along j is safe and profitable.
    vectorize(j, V)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Inner-loop unrolling for reduced overhead
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within each tile, optionally unroll the innermost j-loop by a small
    # factor (e.g., 2 or 4) to reduce loop control overhead and expose
    # more ILP to the compiler. This is orthogonal to vectorization; the
    # compiler can map the unrolled scalar iterations onto SIMD lanes.
    #
    # Let UNROLL_J be a small compile-time constant (e.g., 2 or 4).
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Scalar hoisting of invariant loads (micro-optimizations)
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Example: in the boundary update ey_bc, the value _fict_[t] is invariant
    # across j, so it can be loaded once per time step into a scalar register:
    #
    #   ft = _fict_[t]
    #   for j in [0, ny):
    #       ey[0, j] = ft
    #
    # Compilers typically perform such hoisting automatically; we document
    # it here as part of the intended optimized model.
    #
    # (No explicit directive needed in this DSL; this comment clarifies the
    # expected scalarization.)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. No additional large temporaries
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # We intentionally avoid introducing extra full-size temporary grids
    # (e.g., for intermediate derivatives) to keep memory overhead small.
    # All updates are done in-place on ex, ey, and hz, just as in the original
    # Exo kernel. Any temporaries are limited to register-sized scalars within
    # tiles, so total extra memory usage remains far below the 50% budget.

domain:
    # Time and space dimensions
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)      # time steps
    x: dim in [0, NX)        # spatial index in first dimension
    y: dim in [0, NY)        # spatial index in second dimension

data:
    # All field arrays are stored in separate 2D row-major grids.
    ex[x, y]: inout DATA_TYPE = (x, y) -> x * NY + y   # E-field component
    ey[x, y]: inout DATA_TYPE = (x, y) -> x * NY + y   # E-field component
    hz[x, y]: inout DATA_TYPE = (x, y) -> x * NY + y   # H-field component

    # 1D source term as a function of time, contiguous in memory.
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = t

parameters:
    # Physical scheme coefficients (match original constants).
    ce: DATA_TYPE   # = 0.5  (E-field update coefficient)
    ch: DATA_TYPE   # = 0.7  (H-field update coefficient)

    # Tunable blocking / vectorization parameters (no extra buffers required).
    BX: int         # spatial tile size in x, e.g., 64 or 128
    BY: int         # spatial tile size in y, e.g., 64 or 128
    V:  int         # SIMD width for y (e.g., 4, 8, 16 depending on DATA_TYPE and ISA)

computation:
    # Time-stepping loop is strictly sequential: each step depends on the
    # fields from the previous time step.
    for t in seq([0, TMAX)):

        # 1) Boundary condition on ey at x = 0:
        #    ey(0, y, t+1) = _fict_[t] for all y.
        EY_BND: for y in [0, NY):
            ey[0, y] = _fict_[t]

        # 2) Update interior ey using discrete derivative of hz along x:
        #    ey(x, y, t+1) = ey(x, y, t) - ce * (hz(x, y, t) - hz(x-1, y, t)),
        #    for x in [1, NX), all y.
        EY_UPDATE: for x in [1, NX):
            for y in [0, NY):
                ey[x, y] = ey[x, y] - ce * (hz[x, y] - hz[x - 1, y])

        # 3) Update interior ex using discrete derivative of hz along y:
        #    ex(x, y, t+1) = ex(x, y, t) - ce * (hz(x, y, t) - hz(x, y-1, t)),
        #    for y in [1, NY), all x.
        EX_UPDATE: for x in [0, NX):
            for y in [1, NY):
                ex[x, y] = ex[x, y] - ce * (hz[x, y] - hz[x, y - 1])

        # 4) Update interior hz using curls of ex and ey:
        #    hz(x, y, t+1) = hz(x, y, t) - ch * [
        #        (ex(x, y+1, t+1) - ex(x, y, t+1)) +
        #        (ey(x+1, y, t+1) - ey(x, y, t+1))
        #    ],
        #    for x in [0, NX-1), y in [0, NY-1).
        HZ_UPDATE: for x in [0, NX - 1):
            for y in [0, NY - 1):
                hz[x, y] = hz[x, y] - ch * (
                    (ex[x, y + 1] - ex[x, y]) +
                    (ey[x + 1, y] - ey[x, y])
                )

dependencies:
    # Within each time step, the updates must occur in this order:
    #   1) EY_BND  (sets boundary row of ey)
    #   2) EY_UPDATE (interior ey from hz at previous step)
    #   3) EX_UPDATE (interior ex from hz at previous step)
    #   4) HZ_UPDATE (hz from updated ex and ey at this step)
    for t in [0, TMAX):
        EY_BND(t)    -> EY_UPDATE(t)
        EY_UPDATE(t) -> EX_UPDATE(t)
        EX_UPDATE(t) -> HZ_UPDATE(t)

    # Across time steps, the H-field at time t must be fully updated before
    # any E-field updates at time t+1, because ey/ex at t+1 read hz at time t.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1):
        HZ_UPDATE(t) -> EY_BND(t + 1)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Spatial blocking (tiling) for cache locality
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Block the 2D spatial loops in x and y for all three field updates.
    # This does NOT change the numerical scheme; it only changes the
    # order in which grid points are visited within each time step.
    # Tiles are chosen so that three BX×BY tiles (for ex, ey, hz) fit well
    # in the shared cache of a core or NUMA node.
    block(x, Xb, BX)    # Xb: tile index in x, x: intra-tile coordinate
    block(y, Yb, BY)    # Yb: tile index in y, y: intra-tile coordinate

    # The intended loop structure inside each time step becomes:
    #   for Xb:
    #     for Yb:
    #       for x in [Xb*BX, ...):
    #         for y in [Yb*BY, ...):
    #           <local stencil update>
    # This respects that:
    #   - E-updates (EY_UPDATE, EX_UPDATE) only read hz and their own value.
    #   - H-update (HZ_UPDATE) only reads ex and ey, which are not modified
    #     inside HZ_UPDATE.
    # Hence, reordering across (x, y) within a fixed t is safe.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelism
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelize across spatial tiles in the x-dimension inside each
    # time step. All updates at a fixed t and different (x, y) are
    # pointwise-independent:
    #   - EY_BND writes distinct ey[0, y] for each y.
    #   - EY_UPDATE writes ey[x, y] using only ey[x, y] and hz[*] at time t.
    #   - EX_UPDATE writes ex[x, y] using only ex[x, y] and hz[*] at time t.
    #   - HZ_UPDATE writes hz[x, y] using only ex[*], ey[*] at time t+1.
    # There are no spatial data races, so we can distribute tiles across cores.
    parallelize(Xb)

    # Time dimension t remains strictly sequential and is NOT parallelized,
    # because step t+1 depends on fields produced at step t.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorize along the innermost y-dimension inside each tile. Because
    # the arrays are stored row-major with y as the fastest-varying index,
    # this gives unit-stride accesses for ex[x, y], ey[x, y], and hz[x, y]
    # and for the neighbor accesses used in the stencil.
    vectorize(y, V)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Minor scalar optimizations (conceptual)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # - Hoist _fict_[t] into a scalar f_t before the EY_BND loop:
    #       f_t = _fict_[t]
    #       for y: ey[0, y] = f_t
    #   This avoids reloading the same value for each y.
    #
    # - Treat ce (=0.5) and ch (=0.7) as scalar parameters, possibly
    #   pre-loaded into registers, to make the arithmetic slightly cheaper
    #   and clearer in generated code.
    #
    # These do not change the mathematical computation, only reduce
    # redundant memory traffic and improve constant handling.

domain:
    # Global problem sizes (PolyBench names)
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)          # time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)            # x-direction (row index)
    j: dim in [0, NY)            # y-direction (column index)

data:
    # Electromagnetic field components, stored as 2D row‑major grids.
    # Addressing matches C layout: a[i][j] == a_base[i*NY + j].
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j      # E_x field
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j      # E_y field
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j      # H_z field

    # Time‑varying fictitious source term; 1D array over time.
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

parameters:
    # Physical/stencil coefficients (fixed to match original kernel)
    ce: DATA_TYPE = 0.5          # coefficient used in E‑field updates
    ch: DATA_TYPE = 0.7          # coefficient used in H‑field updates

    # Tunable performance parameters (do not change numerical results)
    TI: int                      # tile size in i (x) dimension, e.g., 32
    TJ: int                      # tile size in j (y) dimension, e.g., 64
    VLEN: int                    # SIMD width for j‑vectorization, e.g., 8 or 16
    TT: int                      # optional time tile size, e.g., 4 (must divide or tile TMAX)

computation:
    # Time stepping is strictly sequential: t depends on all fields at t-1.
    for t in seq([0, TMAX)):

        # 1) Boundary condition on ey at i = 0 for current time t.
        #    This matches: for (j = 0; j < ny; j++) ey[0][j] = _fict_[t];
        ey_bc:
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2) Update ey(i, j) for i >= 1 from hz.
        #    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - 0.5 * (hz[i, j] - hz[i-1, j])
        #    in the original Exo code.
        ey_update:
            for i in [1, NX):
                for j in [0, NY):
                    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - ce * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3) Update ex(i, j) for j >= 1 from hz.
        #    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - 0.5 * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j-1])
        ex_update:
            for i in [0, NX):
                for j in [1, NY):
                    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - ce * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4) Update hz(i, j) from spatial derivatives of ex and ey.
        #    hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - 0.7 * (
        #                   ex[i, j+1] - ex[i, j]
        #                 + ey[i+1, j] - ey[i, j])
        #    Note the interior domain: i in [0, NX-1), j in [0, NY-1).
        hz_update:
            for i in [0, NX - 1):
                for j in [0, NY - 1):
                    hz[i, j] =
                        hz[i, j] - ch * (
                            (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                            (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                        )

dependencies:
    # Time is sequential: each step t+1 depends on the full fields at time t.
    for t in [0, TMAX-1), i in [0, NX), j in [0, NY):
        hz_update(t, i, j) -> ey_bc(t+1, j)
        hz_update(t, i, j) -> ey_update(t+1, i, j)   # via ey[i,j] and hz[i,*]
        hz_update(t, i, j) -> ex_update(t+1, i, j)   # via ex[i,j] and hz[*,j]

    # Within a single time step, updates of ey, ex, and hz at different (i,j)
    # are independent except for the explicit stencil reads:
    #   - ey_update reads hz[i, j] and hz[i-1, j] but does not modify hz
    #   - ex_update reads hz[i, j] and hz[i, j-1] but does not modify hz
    #   - hz_update reads ex and ey but only writes hz[i, j]
    # Therefore, loops on (i,j) at fixed t can be freely tiled, reordered,
    # and parallelized as long as the order between stages (2)->(3)->(4)
    # is preserved and each stage covers its full spatial domain.

optimization:
    # --- Spatial tiling for better cache locality --------------------------------
    # Tile both spatial dimensions of all (i,j) loops to keep working sets
    # in higher cache levels and improve TLB behavior.
    #
    # Applies uniformly to:
    #   ey_update:   i in [1, NX),        j in [0, NY)
    #   ex_update:   i in [0, NX),        j in [1, NY)
    #   hz_update:   i in [0, NX-1),      j in [0, NY-1)
    # and to ey_bc's j‑loop (only 1 row).
    block(i, I, TI)      # i  = I * TI + i_inner
    block(j, J, TJ)      # j  = J * TJ + j_inner
    # Semantics: each original loop over (i,j) is transformed into
    #   for I in tiles_i:
    #     for J in tiles_j:
    #       for i_inner in tile_i(I):
    #         for j_inner in tile_j(J):
    #           body(i, j)
    # with exact coverage of the original index ranges (handling of
    # start offsets like i>=1 or j>=1 is done in the bounds of the
    # inner loops). This reorders (i,j) within a time step but does
    # not change the mathematical result.

    # --- Parallelization over spatial tiles --------------------------------------
    # For fixed time t, there are no write‑after‑read or write‑after‑write
    # dependencies across different rows (i) for any of the three stages:
    #   * ey_update writes ey[i,*], reads only hz[i,*] and hz[i-1,*] (read‑only)
    #   * ex_update writes ex[i,*], reads only hz[i,*] and hz[i,*-1] (read‑only)
    #   * hz_update writes hz[i,*], reads ex and ey but not hz at other i
    # So each tile in I can be computed in parallel at fixed t.
    #
    # Parallelization is coarse‑grained at the tile level to reduce
    # scheduling and synchronization overhead.
    parallelize(I)

    # Time dimension remains purely sequential; DO NOT parallelize t or any of
    # its blocked dimensions. This preserves the explicit time stepping order.

    # --- SIMD vectorization along contiguous j dimension -------------------------
    # The innermost loops after tiling iterate over j_inner with unit stride
    # addressing (row‑major layout), which is ideal for SIMD.
    # The arithmetic is simple (adds, subtracts, FMA‑like patterns),
    # and there are no loop‑carried dependencies along j, so we can
    # safely vectorize j.
    vectorize(j, VLEN)
    # This expresses that the innermost j‑loops in the EY, EX, and HZ updates
    # should be executed using SIMD instructions of width VLEN, with a scalar
    # cleanup for any remainder if NY is not a multiple of VLEN.

    # --- Optional time tiling for improved temporal locality ---------------------
    # For very large TMAX, it can be advantageous to process time in blocks
    # to improve temporal locality of ex/ey/hz in caches, especially when
    # multiple right‑hand sides or multiple domains are processed.
    #
    # We split the sequential time loop into outer time tiles (T_outer)
    # and inner time iterations (t_inner). The overall order of time
    # steps remains t = 0, 1, ..., TMAX-1, so numerical results are
    # unchanged.
    block(t, T_outer, TT)
    # IMPORTANT: T_outer must remain sequential and is NOT parallelized.

    # After time tiling and spatial tiling, the effective loop structure is:
    #   for T_outer in seq(0, ceil(TMAX/TT)):
    #     for t_inner in seq(0, min(TT, TMAX - T_outer*TT)):
    #       for I in parallel tiles over i:
    #         for J in tiles over j:
    #           vectorized j‑inner loops ...
    #
    # which respects all original dependences while improving cache reuse
    # and exploiting thread‑ and SIMD‑level parallelism.

domain:
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)        # physical time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)          # x-direction grid index
    j: dim in [0, NY)          # y-direction grid index

data:
    # 2D fields are stored in row-major order with i as the slow and j as the fast index.
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ex
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ey
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # magnetic field component Hz

    # Time-dependent boundary condition for ey(0, :)
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = t -> t   # 1D array; index is the time step

parameters:
    TMAX: size   # number of time steps
    NX:   size   # grid size in x
    NY:   size   # grid size in y

    # Stencil coefficients; kept as explicit parameters so the implementation
    # can treat them as constants or tune them if needed.
    alpha_e: DATA_TYPE   # usually 0.5 for Ex/Ey updates
    alpha_h: DATA_TYPE   # usually 0.7 for Hz update

    # Tuning knobs for performance (do not affect mathematical result):
    TI: size   # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    TJ: size   # tile size in j (e.g., 32 or 64)
    VJ: size   # SIMD width used for vectorization along j (e.g., 4, 8, or 16)
    UJ: size   # optional unroll factor for inner j loop (small integer, e.g., 2–4)

computation:
    # Time stepping is strictly sequential: each step t reads ex, ey, hz produced
    # at time t-1 and writes the fields for time t.
    for t in seq(0, TMAX):

        # ---- Phase 1: impose Ey boundary condition on the first x-row ----
        # ey(0, j) is set to the time-varying fictitious value _fict_[t] at every j.
        # This uses only data from _fict_ and does not depend on ex, ey, or hz.
        for j in [0, NY):
            ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # ---- Phase 2: update interior of Ey using finite difference in +i direction ----
        # For i >= 1, ey(i, j) is updated from the difference hz(i, j) - hz(i-1, j),
        # using Hz at the previous time level (t), before Hz is updated in Phase 4.
        #
        # Each (i, j) update here:
        #   - reads hz[i, j], hz[i-1, j]
        #   - reads ey[i, j]
        #   - writes ey[i, j]
        # There are no dependencies between distinct (i, j) pairs, so the loop over
        # (i, j) is embarrassingly parallel.
        for i in [1, NX):
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - alpha_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # ---- Phase 3: update interior of Ex using finite difference in +j direction ----
        # For j >= 1, ex(i, j) is updated from the difference hz(i, j) - hz(i, j-1),
        # again using Hz at time level t (not yet updated by Phase 4).
        #
        # Each (i, j) update here:
        #   - reads hz[i, j], hz[i, j-1]
        #   - reads ex[i, j]
        #   - writes ex[i, j]
        # Again, distinct (i, j) iterations are fully independent.
        for i in [0, NX):
            for j in [1, NY):
                ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - alpha_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # ---- Phase 4: update Hz using the discrete curl of E at current time t ----
        # Hz is updated at all interior cells except the last row and last column.
        #
        # Each Hz(i, j) update:
        #   - reads ex[i, j+1], ex[i, j]
        #   - reads ey[i+1, j], ey[i, j]
        #   - reads hz[i, j]
        #   - writes hz[i, j]
        #
        # Ex and Ey used here are the updated fields from Phases 2 and 3 at time t;
        # Hz is updated in place. There are no dependencies between different (i, j)
        # updates within this loop because each iteration reads/writes a unique hz[i, j].
        for i in [0, NX - 1):
            for j in [0, NY - 1):
                hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - alpha_h * (
                                (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                                (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                           )

optimization:
    # All optimizations below preserve semantics because:
    #  - Time dimension t remains strictly sequential.
    #  - Within each phase (2, 3, 4), updates over (i, j) are pointwise and independent.
    #  - Phases are kept in the original order: Ey boundary -> Ey interior -> Ex interior -> Hz.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1) Hoist the time-dependent boundary scalar out of the boundary loop
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Implementation detail: load _fict_[t] once into a scalar b_t, and use b_t
    # inside the boundary j-loop. This avoids redundant loads and encourages the
    # compiler to keep the value in a register.
    #
    # Semantically:
    #   let b_t = _fict_[t]
    #   for j in [0, NY): ey[0, j] = b_t
    #
    # No separate directive form is needed; this is a local scalar hoisting.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2) Tile the 2-D spatial loops for cache locality
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # We tile the (i, j) iteration space in Phases 2–4. For each fixed t,
    # each phase becomes:
    #   for Ii in [0, NX) step TI:
    #       for Jj in [0, NY) step TJ:
    #           for i in [Ii, min(Ii+TI, NX)):
    #               for j in [Jj, min(Jj+TJ, NY)):
    #                   ... original stencil update ...
    #
    # Because there are no loop-carried dependences across different (i, j),
    # this blocking is semantics-equivalent and improves spatial and temporal
    # locality for ex, ey, and hz within each tile.
    #
    # TI, TJ are tunable; they should be chosen so that three tiles
    # (for ex, ey, hz) comfortably fit in the last-level cache.
    block(i, Ii, TI)   # strip-mine outer i into tile index Ii and intra-tile i
    block(j, Jj, TJ)   # strip-mine outer j into tile index Jj and intra-tile j
    hoist(Ii)          # reorder loops so Ii and Jj become outer loops
    hoist(Jj)

    # The above 'block' and 'hoist' transformations are applied to the
    # (i, j) loops of Phases 2, 3, and 4 only. The boundary loop (Phase 1)
    # has no i-dimension and is left untouched.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3) Parallelize across spatial tiles
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within a fixed time step t and a given phase:
    #   - each tile (Ii, Jj) updates a disjoint subset of grid points;
    #   - there are no writes that cross tile boundaries within that phase;
    #   - Hz is not updated until Phase 4, so the Ey/Ex phases are read-only
    #     with respect to hz.
    #
    # Therefore, we can safely parallelize over the outer tile index Ii
    # (and optionally Jj) in each phase using, for example, OpenMP.
    #
    # This achieves spatial domain decomposition over cores while preserving
    # the sequential dependence across time steps t.
    parallelize(Ii)    # e.g., '#pragma omp parallel for' on the loop over Ii

    # Note: we intentionally do NOT parallelize over t, because each time step
    # depends on the updated ex, ey, hz from the previous step.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4) Vectorize the innermost j loop
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Arrays are row-major with j as the fastest index, so accesses ex[i, j],
    # ey[i, j], hz[i, j] in all phases are contiguous in memory along j.
    #
    # We therefore vectorize the innermost j loop inside each tile. VJ is
    # the SIMD width (e.g., 4 for SSE/AVX single precision, 8 for AVX2,
    # 16 for AVX-512).
    #
    # The compiler can then use vector loads/stores and FMA instructions
    # for each stencil update.
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5) Unroll the inner j loop within tiles (optional)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # To increase instruction-level parallelism (ILP) and hide latencies,
    # we can unroll the innermost j loop by a small factor UJ (e.g., 2–4).
    # Since iterations over j are independent within each phase, unrolling
    # is semantics-preserving.
    unroll(j, UJ)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6) No extra large temporaries
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # All optimizations above operate in-place on ex, ey, hz and introduce at
    # most a few scalar temporaries (e.g., b_t, local differences). No extra
    # 2D or 3D buffers are allocated, so the memory footprint remains within
    # the original plus negligible scalar overhead (<< 50% increase).

domain:
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)          # time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)            # first spatial dimension
    j: dim in [0, NY)            # second spatial dimension

data:
    # Row-major 2D fields: (i, j) -> linear offset
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j

    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t     # time-dependent boundary term

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (symbolic here; in PolyBench they are compile-time constants).
    TMAX: size
    NX: size
    NY: size

    # Tunable performance parameters.
    Ti: size        # spatial tile size in i (e.g., 16, 32, 64)
    Tj: size        # spatial tile size in j (e.g., 32, 64, 128)
    VEC_J: size     # vector width along j (e.g., 4, 8, 16 depending on DATA_TYPE and ISA)
    UNROLL_J: size  # optional extra unroll factor along j (typically 1, 2, 4, or 8)

computation:
    # Time stepping is explicit and sequential.
    for t in seq(0, TMAX):

        # 1. Boundary condition on ey at i = 0:
        #    ey(0, j, t) = _fict_[t] for all j.
        Ey_boundary(t):
            # (Implementation-level optimization: hoist _fict_[t] into a scalar tmp_fict
            #  outside the j-loop; see optimization section.)
            for j in seq(0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2. Update ey using finite difference of hz along i.
        #    For i >= 1:
        #      ey(i, j, t) = ey(i, j, t) - 0.5 * (hz(i, j, t-1) - hz(i-1, j, t-1))
        Ey_update(t):
            for i in seq(1, NX), j in seq(0, NY):
                ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - 0.5 * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3. Update ex using finite difference of hz along j.
        #    For j >= 1:
        #      ex(i, j, t) = ex(i, j, t) - 0.5 * (hz(i, j, t-1) - hz(i, j-1, t-1))
        Ex_update(t):
            for i in seq(0, NX), j in seq(1, NY):
                ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - 0.5 * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4. Update hz using curls of ex and ey:
        #    hz(i, j, t) = hz(i, j, t-1)
        #                  - 0.7 * ( (ex(i, j+1, t) - ex(i, j, t))
        #                           + (ey(i+1, j, t) - ey(i, j, t)) )
        Hz_update(t):
            for i in seq(0, NX - 1), j in seq(0, NY - 1):
                hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - 0.7 * (
                    (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                    (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                )

dependencies:
    # Cross-time dependencies: t is strictly sequential.
    # ex, ey, hz at time t+1 depend on hz at time t, so we cannot
    # parallelize across t without more involved wavefront transformations.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1), i in [0, NX), j in [0, NY):
        Hz_update(t, i, j) -> Ey_update(t + 1, i, j)   # hz used in ey-update at next step
        Hz_update(t, i, j) -> Ex_update(t + 1, i, j)   # hz used in ex-update at next step

    # Within a single time step t:
    # - Ey_update and Ex_update read hz but do not modify it.
    #   Their iterations over (i, j) are mutually independent.
    # - Hz_update reads ex and ey and writes hz. Its iterations over (i, j) are
    #   independent once ex and ey for this time step are available.
    for t in [0, TMAX), i in [0, NX - 1), j in [0, NY - 1):
        # Hz at (i, j) uses ex(i, j) and ex(i, j+1)
        Ex_update(t, i, j)   -> Hz_update(t, i, j)
        Ex_update(t, i, j+1) -> Hz_update(t, i, j)

        # Hz at (i, j) uses ey(i, j) and ey(i+1, j)
        Ey_update(t, i, j)   -> Hz_update(t, i, j)
        Ey_update(t, i+1, j) -> Hz_update(t, i, j)

    # Boundary injections must precede any use of ey[0, j] at time t.
    for t in [0, TMAX), j in [0, NY):
        Ey_boundary(t, j) -> Hz_update(t, 0, j)   # hz(0, j) uses ey(0, j) and ey(1, j)

optimization:
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Spatial blocking for cache locality
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Apply 2D blocking (tiling) in (i, j) for all three spatial sweeps
    # Ey_update, Ex_update, and Hz_update (the loops that have both i and j).
    #
    # block(D, TD, S) logically transforms:
    #   for D in [0, N):
    #       body(D)
    # into:
    #   for TD in [0, ceil(N / S)):
    #       for D in [TD * S, min(N, (TD + 1) * S)):
    #           body(D)
    #
    # We choose tiles of size (Ti, Tj) so that ex, ey, hz tiles fit in L1/L2.
    block(i, I, Ti)     # tile i into outer tile index I and inner i
    block(j, J, Tj)     # tile j into outer tile index J and inner j

    # Move the tile loops I, J to be just inside the time loop so that the
    # execution order for each sweep becomes:
    #   for t:
    #     for I:
    #       for J:
    #         for i in tile(I):
    #           for j in tile(J):
    #             update(...)
    #
    # This preserves the original sequential dependence in t and all
    # pointwise spatial dependencies, while improving spatial locality.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelism
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within a fixed time step t and a fixed spatial sweep (Ey_update,
    # Ex_update, Hz_update), each (I, J) tile is independent of the others.
    #
    # We parallelize over I (tiles in the i direction); an implementation
    # would map this to an OpenMP-style parallel for over I inside the
    # time loop, reusing the parallel region across the three sweeps.
    parallelize(I)

    # (If desired, a more aggressive strategy is to parallelize over both
    # I and J with a 2D schedule, but parallelizing only I already exposes
    # ample coarse-grain parallelism on a 32-core machine while keeping
    # scheduling simple.)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # All arrays are row-major with j as the fastest-varying index, so
    # iterating with j innermost gives contiguous memory access and is ideal
    # for SIMD vectorization.
    #
    # We vectorize the inner j-loop in each tiled sweep.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # Optionally unroll the j-loop further to reduce loop overhead and
    # increase ILP inside each vectorized chunk. UNROLL_J is chosen so that
    # VEC_J * UNROLL_J is still small enough to keep register pressure
    # reasonable (e.g., UNROLL_J = 1–4).
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Scalar hoisting / invariant code motion
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # In Ey_boundary, the value _fict_[t] is invariant across j:
    #   for j: ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]
    #
    # We hoist this load into a scalar tmp_fict once per time step:
    #
    #   tmp_fict = _fict_[t]
    #   for j: ey[0, j] = tmp_fict
    #
    # This avoids reloading _fict_[t] ny times and makes it easy for the
    # compiler to vectorize the boundary fill as a simple broadcast store.
    # Conceptually:
    #   hoist(_fict_[t] into scalar tmp_fict in Ey_boundary)
    #
    # (This does not change semantics and introduces only O(1) extra storage.)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Notes
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # - We deliberately keep the time loop sequential to respect the stencil’s
    #   cross-time dependencies.
    # - We do not introduce extra full-sized temporary fields, so peak memory
    #   usage remains essentially the same as the original (well within the
    #   +50% budget).
    # - Applying the same tiling and vectorization scheme to all three spatial
    #   sweeps keeps the access patterns regular and predictable for the
    #   backend compiler and hardware prefetchers.
